s0.name: Matrix toolkit
s0.blurb: The vocabulary every later formula is written in. $\hat\beta=(X'X)^{-1}X'y$ uses dimensions, multiplication, transposes, rank and inverses, all in one line.
s0.metaphor: A matrix is an **egg carton**: a grid of slots, described by **rows × columns** (always in that order, like reading a page top-to-bottom then left-to-right). A vector is a carton with a single row or a single column of slots.

topics.title: Shapes: rows × columns
topics.html:
The dimension of a matrix is (number of rows) × (number of columns). Say it out loud as "R by C".

ObjectLooks likeDimension
Scalar$7$$1\times1$
Column vector$\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}$$3\times1$
Row vector$\begin{bmatrix}2&4&6\end{bmatrix}$$1\times3$
Matrix$\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 & 5 \\ 2 & 4 & 6\end{bmatrix}$$2\times3$

In econometrics, vectors are columns by default. $y$ is $n\times1$, one row per observation.

topics.title: Adding and scaling
topics.html:
Adding/subtracting works slot by slot, like stacking two egg cartons on top of each other. That only works if the cartons have exactly the same shape.

Scalar multiplication multiplies every slot: $2\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -4 \\ 6 & 8\end{bmatrix}$.

Exam trap
A $2\times3$ plus a $3\times2$ is not defined. Same number of entries isn't enough; the shapes must match.

topics.title: Multiplying matrices
topics.html:
Write the two dimensions side by side. The inner numbers must match (they "shake hands" and disappear), and the outer numbers give the size of the answer:

$$(\underbrace{4\times 3}_{A})(\underbrace{3\times 2}_{B})=\;4\times 2$$

Each entry of the result is a row of the first × a column of the second: multiply pairwise and add (an inner product).

Try itWill these multiply?
Try itRow × column, step by step (bank Q6)
Not commutative
Order matters: $AB\neq BA$ in general. Putting on socks then shoes is not the same as shoes then socks. Often $BA$ isn't even defined.

topics.title: Transpose: flip over the diagonal
topics.html:
$A'$ turns rows into columns: row 1 of $A$ becomes column 1 of $A'$. An $m\times n$ matrix becomes $n\times m$.

$$A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6\end{bmatrix}\quad\Rightarrow\quad A'=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \\ 3 & 6\end{bmatrix}$$
Socks-and-shoes rule
$(AB)'=B'A'$ and $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$. Undoing a sequence reverses its order. Also $(A')'=A$.
Exam trap
Writing $1,2,3,4,5,6$ in reading order into a $3\times2$ grid gives $\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \\ 5 & 6\end{bmatrix}$, which is not the transpose.

topics.title: Inner product and orthogonality
topics.html:
$x'y=x_1y_1+x_2y_2+\cdots+x_ny_n$: multiply matching entries, then add. The result is a single number.

If $x'y=0$ the vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular arrows). Example: $(1,2)\cdot(2,-1)=2-2=0$.

Where it comes back
$E[Y]=y'p$ (Seminar 1) and $e'e=\sum e_i^2$ (Seminar 2) are both inner products. The outer product $ee'$ (Seminar 3) is the opposite: a column times a row, which gives a whole matrix.

topics.title: Linear combinations, span, independence
topics.html:
A linear combination is a recipe: $a_1x_1+a_2x_2$ ("2 scoops of $x_1$, minus 1 scoop of $x_2$"). The span is every dish you could ever cook with those ingredients.

  • Two arrows pointing in different directions: the span is the whole plane $\mathbb{R}^2$.
  • Two arrows on the same line ($x_2=2x_1$): you're stuck on that line.
Try itMix two vectors

Linearly independent: the only recipe that gives the zero vector is "use zero of everything" ($a_1=\dots=a_k=0$). If you can write one vector as a remix of the others (e.g. $x_3=2x_1+x_2$), they're dependent.

topics.title: Rank
topics.html:
Rank = number of independent directions among the columns (equivalently, the rows).

$$\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}:\ \text{column 2}=2\times\text{column 1}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{rank}=1$$

A $k$-column matrix with rank $k$ has full (column) rank. In regression that means no regressor is an exact combination of the others.

topics.title: Identity and inverse
topics.html:
$I$ (1s on the diagonal, 0s elsewhere) is "multiply by 1": $AI=IA=A$.

The inverse is an undo button: $AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I$. A square matrix has an inverse exactly when it has full rank. With dependent columns there's no undo, because information was lost.

Why OLS cares
$\hat\beta=(X'X)^{-1}X'y$ needs $(X'X)^{-1}$ to exist, so $X$ must have full column rank. That is the no-perfect-multicollinearity assumption.

patterns.title: Read a dimension / identify a vector
patterns.recipe: Rows first, columns second. A column vector is $n\times1$. Transposing swaps the two numbers.

patterns.title: Is it defined? What size is the product?
patterns.recipe: Addition needs identical shapes. Multiplication needs the inner numbers to match, and the answer takes the outer numbers.

patterns.title: Compute: scalar multiple, product, combination
patterns.recipe: Scalar: every entry. Product: row·column for each entry. Combination: scale each vector, then add or subtract entry by entry.

patterns.title: Transpose rules
patterns.recipe: Rows become columns. $(AB)'=B'A'$, reversing the order.

patterns.title: Inner product and orthogonality
patterns.recipe: Multiply matching entries and add. A result of $0$ means orthogonal.

patterns.title: Span, independence, rank, inverse
patterns.recipe: Is one vector a multiple or combination of the others? If yes: dependent, the span shrinks, rank < k, and there's no inverse.

s1.name: Expected value & conditional expectations
s1.blurb: Regression is built from averages: the overall average $E[Y]$, the group averages $E[Y\mid X]$, and how the two connect.
s1.metaphor: $E[Y]$ is the **balance point of a seesaw**. Each possible value sits on the plank, and its probability is how heavy it is. Heavier (more likely) values pull the balance point towards themselves.

topics.title: Kinds of data (and a few key words)
topics.html:
TypePicture it asExample
Cross-sectionOne photo of many units at one moment526 workers in 1976 (WAGE1)
Time seriesA video of one unit over timeUzbekistan's GDP 2000–2025
Pooled cross-sectionsSeveral photos of different crowds in different yearsHouse sales in 1978 and in 1981 (KIELMC)
Panel (longitudinal)A video of the same crowdSame firms followed every year
  • Experimental data: the researcher assigns treatment (ideally at random) to estimate a causal effect. Observational data: no intervention.
  • Random sampling: a fair lottery where every member of the population is equally likely to be picked.
  • Ceteris paribus: "all else equal". Change one factor and freeze every other relevant factor.

topics.title: Expected value = probability-weighted average
topics.html:
$$E[Y]=\sum_y y\,P(Y=y)=y'p$$
Example (seminar)
$Y\in\{50,70,90\}$ with probabilities $0.2, 0.5, 0.3$: $E[Y]=50(0.2)+70(0.5)+90(0.3)=10+35+27=72$.
Exam trap
The plain average of the values, $(50+70+90)/3=70$, ignores the probabilities. The bank always offers it as a distractor.

topics.title: Rules that save time
topics.html:
RuleIn words
$E[c]=c$A constant's average is itself
$E[a+bY]=a+bE[Y]$Constants pass straight through
$E[a+bX+cY]=a+bE[X]+cE[Y]$Works without independence
$E[Y-E[Y]]=0$Deviations from the mean balance out
Bank Q5
$E[X]=4,\ E[Y]=6$: $E[5+2X-3Y]=5+8-18=-5$. Keep the signs.

topics.title: Joint, marginal and conditional probability
topics.html:
A joint table gives $P(Y=y, X=x)$ for every pair, and all the cells sum to 1.

  • Marginal $P(X=0)$: add the whole column. These totals are literally written in the table's margins.
  • Conditional $P(Y=y\mid X=x)=\dfrac{P(Y=y,X=x)}{P(X=x)}$: zoom into one column and rescale it so it sums to 1.
Try itZoom into a column

topics.title: Conditional expectation $E[Y\mid X=x]$
topics.html:
Exactly the same weighted average, but using the conditional probabilities: the average of $Y$ inside one group.

From raw data (the income–consumption tables), $E[Y\mid X=120]$ means: take only the rows with income 120 and average their consumption.

Bank Q14
Income 120: consumption 79, 89, 90, so $E[Y\mid X=120]=258/3=86.00$.
Exam trap
83.67 is the average of all nine people, i.e. $E[Y]$, not $E[Y\mid X=120]$. The other group means (58.67, 106.33) are also offered.

topics.title: Law of Iterated Expectations
topics.html:
$$E[Y]=E\big[E[Y\mid X]\big]=\sum_x E[Y\mid X=x]\,P(X=x)$$

The school average is the class averages weighted by class size. A big class pulls the school average towards its own mean.

Bank Q13
$60(0.7)+80(0.3)=42+24=66$. The trap answer 70 weights the two groups equally.

topics.title: From $E[Y\mid X]$ to regression and the error term
topics.html:
Join the group averages and you get the conditional expectation function (the population regression line). Each person's gap from their group average is the error term:

$$u=Y-E[Y\mid X]\qquad(\text{everything else that moves }Y)$$
Try itPopulation regression function (seminar Q4 data)

topics.title: Why $E[Y\mid X]$ isn't automatically causal
topics.html:
Ice-cream sales and drownings move together because summer drives both. That's a confounder. And sometimes $Y$ causes $X$ (reverse causality).

So a conditional mean describes association. Causal claims need a design or assumptions that rule these out (Seminar 4 makes this precise).

patterns.title: Data types and definitions
patterns.recipe: Photo (cross-section), video of one unit (time series), photos of different crowds (pooled), video of the same crowd (panel).

patterns.title: Compute $E[Y]$ from a table
patterns.recipe: Multiply each value by its probability and add.

patterns.title: Linearity of expectation
patterns.recipe: $E[a+bX+cY]=a+bE[X]+cE[Y]$. Constants come out, signs stay, no independence needed.

patterns.title: Marginal and conditional probability
patterns.recipe: Marginal = column sum. Conditional = cell ÷ column sum.

patterns.title: Conditional expectation
patterns.recipe: Average within the group only: with conditional probabilities, or with the raw rows for that $X$.

patterns.title: Law of Iterated Expectations
patterns.recipe: Weight each group mean by its group probability.

patterns.title: Error term and causality
patterns.recipe: $u$ = all omitted influences. $E[Y\mid X]$ isn't causal because of confounders and reverse causality.

s2.name: OLS in matrix form
s2.blurb: Where $\hat\beta=(X'X)^{-1}X'y$ comes from, which assumption buys what, and how to tell the population error from the residual.
s2.metaphor: Imagine a stiff rod (the fitted line) tied to each data point with **rubber bands**. The rod settles where the total stretch (measured as **squared** length) is smallest. That resting place is OLS.

topics.title: The model in matrix clothes
topics.html:
$$\underbrace{y}_{n\times1}=\underbrace{X}_{n\times k}\ \underbrace{\beta}_{k\times1}+\underbrace{\varepsilon}_{n\times1}$$

$X$ has one row per observation and one column per coefficient, including a column of 1s for the constant. So "a constant and three regressors" means $k=4$.

Shortcut
$X'X$ and $(X'X)^{-1}$ are always $k\times k$. $X'y$ and $\hat\beta$ are $k\times1$. $n$ never appears in them.

topics.title: Population error $\varepsilon$ vs residual $e$
topics.html:
$\varepsilon=y-X\beta$$e=y-X\hat\beta$
Usestrue $\beta$estimated $\hat\beta$
Observed?NeverYes, after estimation
Lives inPopulationSample

Think of $\varepsilon$ as the true wind gust that pushed each dart, and $e$ as how far each dart landed from where you aimed. You can measure the second; you can only guess at the first.

topics.title: Least squares: smallest total square area
topics.html:
OLS picks $\hat\beta$ to minimise $e'e=\sum e_i^2$. Residuals are squared so that $+5$ and $-5$ can't cancel into a fake "perfect fit". Below, each residual is drawn as an actual square: OLS makes their total area as small as possible.

Try itMake the squares as small as you can

Comparing two candidate $\hat\beta$'s? The one with the smaller $e'e$ fits better.

topics.title: Three derivative rules (that's all you need)
topics.html:
Type of termScalar versionMatrix version
Constant (no $\beta$)$\frac{d}{dx}c=0$$\frac{\partial\, y'y}{\partial\beta}=0$
Linear$\frac{d}{dx}ax=a$$\frac{\partial\,\beta'a}{\partial\beta}=a$, so $\frac{\partial(-2\beta'X'y)}{\partial\beta}=-2X'y$
Quadratic$\frac{d}{dx}ax^2=2ax$$\frac{\partial\,\beta'A\beta}{\partial\beta}=2A\beta$, so $\frac{\partial\,\beta'X'X\beta}{\partial\beta}=2X'X\beta$

topics.title: Deriving $\hat\beta$ step by step
topics.html: Try itClick through the derivation

topics.title: Full rank (no perfect multicollinearity)
topics.html:
$\operatorname{rank}(X)=k$: no column is an exact combination of the others. Then $X'X$ is invertible and there is one unique $\hat\beta$.

It fails if, e.g., $x_3=x_1+x_2$, or with all category dummies plus a constant (Seminar 5). Two GPS beacons in the same spot can't triangulate your position: the data can't separate the two effects.

topics.title: Unbiasedness
topics.html:
$$\hat\beta=(X'X)^{-1}X'(X\beta+\varepsilon)=\beta+(X'X)^{-1}X'\varepsilon$$

Take $E(\cdot\mid X)$: the second term vanishes if $E(\varepsilon\mid X)=0$. Then $E(\hat\beta)=\beta$: the darts are centred on the bullseye on average, even though each throw misses a little.

AssumptionBuys you
Linear model $y=X\beta+\varepsilon$Defines what we estimate
Full rank$(X'X)^{-1}$ exists, so $\hat\beta$ is unique
$E(\varepsilon\mid X)=0$Unbiasedness
Exam trap
Homoskedasticity and normality are not needed for unbiasedness. Example of failure: motivation drives both attendance and scores but is omitted, so $E(\varepsilon\mid X)\neq0$.

topics.title: Mechanical facts about residuals
topics.html:
The normal equations say $X'(y-X\hat\beta)=X'e=0$. This always holds by construction. With a constant (a column of 1s), it implies $\sum e_i=0$, so the residuals average zero.

Exam trap
$X'e=0$ is a sample identity. It does not prove the population assumption $E(\varepsilon\mid X)=0$.

patterns.title: Objects and dimensions
patterns.recipe: $k$ = constant + slopes. $X$: $n\times k$, $\beta$: $k\times1$, $X'X$: $k\times k$, $X'y$: $k\times1$.

patterns.title: Residual vs error, the objective
patterns.recipe: $e=y-X\hat\beta$. Minimise $e'e$ (smaller is better). Square so signs can't cancel.

patterns.title: Matrix derivatives
patterns.recipe: Constant → 0. Linear $\beta'a$ → $a$. Quadratic $\beta'A\beta$ → $2A\beta$.

patterns.title: Derivation chain
patterns.recipe: Expand, then FOC $-2X'y+2X'X\hat\beta=0$, then $X'X\hat\beta=X'y$, then $\hat\beta=(X'X)^{-1}X'y$.

patterns.title: Full rank
patterns.recipe: An exact linear combination among regressors means rank < k, no inverse, no unique solution.

patterns.title: Unbiasedness and residual properties
patterns.recipe: $\hat\beta=\beta+(X'X)^{-1}X'\varepsilon$. You need $E(\varepsilon\mid X)=0$. Residuals sum to 0 when there's a constant.

s3.name: Standard errors
s3.blurb: How uncertain is $\hat\beta$? Variance rules → the sandwich formula → $\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}$ → standard errors → $t$-tests.
s3.metaphor: Your coefficient is **one arrow** on a target. If you could redo the whole study with a fresh sample, the arrow would land somewhere slightly different. The **standard error** measures how widely those arrows would scatter: small se, tight cluster.

topics.title: $ee'$ and $\Omega$: the errors' fingerprint
topics.html:
The outer product $ee'$ is $n\times n$. Its diagonal holds $e_i^2$ (how big each error is), and its off-diagonal holds $e_ie_j$ (whether errors move together).

The population version is $\Omega=\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon\mid X)$:

Try itThree kinds of Ω
Exam trap
One sample's $e_1e_2\neq0$ proves nothing. Even uncorrelated errors almost never multiply to exactly zero. Heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation are properties of the population $\Omega$.

topics.title: Variance rules
topics.html:
RuleWhy
$\operatorname{Var}(c)=0$A constant doesn't vary
$\operatorname{Var}(Y+c)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)$Moving everyone up 10 points doesn't change the spread
$\operatorname{Var}(aY)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)$Stretching is squared, so the sign disappears
$sd(aY+c)=|a|\,sd(Y)$SD is the square root: no squaring
$\operatorname{Var}(aY+bZ)=a^2V_Y+b^2V_Z+2ab\,\operatorname{Cov}$watch the sign of $ab$
$\operatorname{Var}(Az\mid X)=A\operatorname{Var}(z\mid X)A'$the matrix "$a^2$" is a sandwich
Bank Q11
$\operatorname{Var}(2Y-Z)$ with $V_Y=4,V_Z=9,\operatorname{Cov}=1$: $a=2,b=-1$ gives $16+9+2(2)(-1)(1)=21$.
Exam trap
$\operatorname{Var}(2Y-Z)$ is not $16-9$. Variances always add; only the covariance term can subtract.

topics.title: Deriving $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta\mid X)$
topics.html:
1
$\hat\beta-\beta=(X'X)^{-1}X'\varepsilon=A\varepsilon$, with $A=(X'X)^{-1}X'$ fixed given $X$.
2
$\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta\mid X)=\operatorname{Var}(A\varepsilon\mid X)=A\,\Omega\,A'$
3
$=(X'X)^{-1}X'\,\Omega\,X(X'X)^{-1}$, the sandwich: bread–meat–bread.
4
If $\Omega=\sigma^2I$: $\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}X'X(X'X)^{-1}=\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}$.

The result is $k\times k$. The diagonal holds each coefficient's variance; the off-diagonals hold covariances.

topics.title: From $\hat\sigma^2$ to a standard error
topics.html:
$$\hat\sigma^2=\frac{e'e}{n-k},\qquad \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta_j)=\hat\sigma^2\,[(X'X)^{-1}]_{jj},\qquad se(\hat\beta_j)=\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\beta_j)}$$
Bank Q22–24
$e'e=150,\ n=80,\ k=5\Rightarrow\hat\sigma^2=150/75=2$. With $\hat\sigma^2=4$ and $[(X'X)^{-1}]_{22}=0.16$: variance $=0.64$, so $se=0.80$.
Exam trap
$k$ counts the intercept. The usual wrong answers divide by $n$ (1.875) or take $\sqrt{0.16}=0.40$ without multiplying by $\hat\sigma^2$.

In Stata output, $\hat\sigma=$ Root MSE.

topics.title: What a standard error means (simulation)
topics.html:
The seminar simulation: the true model is $y=2+3x+u$. Draw many samples, run OLS on each, and look at the spread of the $\hat\beta_2$'s.

Try itRepeat the study 1,000 times
What shrinks the se
Smaller error variance $\sigma^2$, more observations, and more spread in $X$ (a longer lever pins the slope down). Adding irrelevant or collinear regressors raises it. A standard error is never negative.

topics.title: The partial significance $t$-test
topics.html:
$$H_0:\beta_j=0\quad\text{vs}\quad H_1:\beta_j\neq0,\qquad t=\frac{\hat\beta_j}{se(\hat\beta_j)}$$

Reject $H_0$ if $|t|$ is large (roughly $>2$ at 5%) or, equivalently, if $p<\alpha$. It's "partial" because the other regressors are held constant.

Try itt-statistic and decision
Reading the hypotheses in words
$H_0:\beta_2=0$: "$X_2$ has no effect on the expected value of $Y$". $H_1$: "$X_2$ has an effect". It's the variable that has the effect; $\beta_2$ is its size.

topics.title: Heteroskedasticity: what breaks, what doesn't
topics.html:
Under heteroskedasticity
Coefficients $\hat\beta$Still unbiased (only needs $E(u\mid X)=0$)
Usual se $\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}$Wrong: it assumed $\Omega=\sigma^2I$
$t$-tests, $p$-valuesUnreliable unless robust se are used
$R^2$Still computable

patterns.title: Outer product and Ω patterns
patterns.recipe: Diagonal = variances (equal: homoskedastic; different: heteroskedastic). Off-diagonal ≠ 0: autocorrelation. One sample proves nothing.

patterns.title: Variance and SD rules
patterns.recipe: Shift: no change. Scale: $a^2$ (SD: $|a|$). Two variables: $a^2V_Y+b^2V_Z+2ab\operatorname{Cov}$.

patterns.title: Sandwich derivation
patterns.recipe: $\hat\beta-\beta=A\varepsilon$, so $A\Omega A'$; with $\Omega=\sigma^2I$ you get $\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}$ ($k\times k$).

patterns.title: $\hat\sigma^2$ and se calculations
patterns.recipe: $e'e/(n-k)$, then $\times$ the diagonal entry, then $\sqrt{\ }$.

patterns.title: $t$-statistics and $p$-value decisions
patterns.recipe: $t=\hat\beta/se$. Reject if $p<\alpha$. The variable $X$ has the effect; $\beta$ is its size.

patterns.title: Meaning of se and heteroskedasticity
patterns.recipe: se = sampling uncertainty. It shrinks with $n$ and spread in $X$. Heteroskedasticity breaks the usual se, not unbiasedness.

s4.name: Controls & model fit
s4.blurb: What "controlling for" really does (FWL), which controls belong in a model (causal diagrams), and how to judge fit ($R^2$) and joint significance ($F$).
s4.metaphor: Controlling for $z$ is like **noise-cancelling headphones**. First cancel out everything $z$ can explain in both $y$ and $x$. Whatever is left is $x$'s *own* voice, and the coefficient is how $y$'s leftover responds to $x$'s leftover.

topics.title: Frisch–Waugh–Lovell: what “controlling for” means
topics.html:
1
Regress $x$ on $z$ and keep the residual $r_x$: the part of $x$ that $z$ can't explain.
2
Regress $y$ on $z$ and keep the residual $r_y$.
3
Regress $r_y$ on $r_x$. The slope equals $\hat\beta_1$ from $y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2z+u$.
Checked in real data (WAGE1)
reg wage educ exper gives educ = 0.6442721. The FWL route (partial exper out of both) gives exactly 0.6442721.
Exam trap
FWL returns the multiple-regression coefficient (FoS: 0.097), not the simple one (0.219).

topics.title: Why coefficients move when you add a control
topics.html:
After adding $z$, OLS only uses the variation in $x$ that's not shared with $z$. Math and IELTS overlap (good students do well at both), so once IELTS is held fixed, Math's coefficient drops from 0.219 to 0.097.

Coefficients can also rise: in WAGE1, educ goes from 0.54 to 0.64 once exper is added, because more educated workers have less experience.

Interpretation
$\beta_1$ in a multiple regression is a partial (ceteris paribus) association, holding the other regressors fixed. It is causal only if the right controls are in and the wrong ones are out.

topics.title: Confounder, mediator, collider
topics.html:
Try itThe three shapes to recognise
Mediator arithmetic (bank Q12)
Total effect = direct + (product along the indirect path) $=1+0.8\times2=2.6$. Controlling for $M$ leaves only the direct effect, about 1.
Try itConditioning on a collider creates a fake link
Rule of thumb
Choose controls by their role in the causal diagram, not because they're available or "make things significant".

topics.title: $R^2$: share of the variation explained
topics.html:
$$R^2=1-\frac{RSS}{TSS},\qquad RSS=\sum e_i^2,\quad TSS=\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2$$

Picture $TSS$ as a whole pie of variation in $y$. $RSS$ is the slice the model failed to explain. $R^2=0.40$ means 40% of the sample variation in $y$ is explained.

Exam trap
$RSS/TSS$ (e.g. 0.60 or 0.49) is the unexplained share. Also: a high $R^2$ doesn't prove causality, a low $R^2$ doesn't make coefficients insignificant, and $R^2$ never falls when you add a regressor.

topics.title: Adjusted $R^2$
topics.html:
$$\bar R^2=1-\frac{RSS/(n-k)}{TSS/(n-1)}$$

It charges a "fee" for each regressor, so it can fall (even go negative) when a useless variable is added. It's always $\le R^2$ and still says nothing about causality.

Bank Q23
$n=100,k=5,RSS=300,TSS=500$: $\frac{300/95}{500/99}=0.625$, so $\bar R^2=0.375$ (just below $R^2=0.40$).

topics.title: The overall $F$ test
topics.html:
$$H_0:\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_{k-1}=0,\qquad F=\frac{R^2/(k-1)}{(1-R^2)/(n-k)}$$

It asks whether all the slopes are jointly zero, i.e. whether the model explains nothing. Large $F$ (or small Prob > F) means reject.

Bank Q25
$\frac{0.40/4}{0.60/95}=15.83$.

topics.title: The partial $F$ test
topics.html:
Tests a group of coefficients, e.g. $H_0:\beta_3=\beta_4=0$ ($q=2$ restrictions), while the other variables stay in the model.

ModelContains$R^2$
Unrestrictedeverything, including the tested variableslarger
Restricteddrops the tested variables (imposes $H_0$)smaller
$$F=\frac{(R^2_{ur}-R^2_r)/q}{(1-R^2_{ur})/(n-k_{ur})}$$

Reject if $F>F_{crit}$ or Prob > F $<\alpha$. Variables can be jointly significant even if none is individually significant.

Try itFit and F calculator

patterns.title: FWL mechanics
patterns.recipe: Partial the control out of both $y$ and $x$, then regress residual on residual. The slope is the same as in the full regression.

patterns.title: Interpreting controls
patterns.recipe: Partial association holding the others fixed. Coefficients move because shared variation is removed. Choose controls by causal role.

patterns.title: Causal diagrams
patterns.recipe: $X\leftarrow C\to Y$ confounder (control it). $X\to M\to Y$ mediator (don't control it for the total effect). $X\to C\leftarrow Y$ collider (don't control it: a fake, usually negative, link appears).

patterns.title: $R^2$ calculations and meaning
patterns.recipe: $1-RSS/TSS$. It measures fit, not causation, and never falls when a regressor is added.

patterns.title: Adjusted $R^2$
patterns.recipe: $1-\frac{RSS/(n-k)}{TSS/(n-1)}$. It penalizes regressors.

patterns.title: $F$ tests
patterns.recipe: Overall: all slopes $=0$, using $k-1$ and $n-k$. Partial: $q$ = number of restrictions. Reject if $F>F_{crit}$.

s5.name: Dummies, interactions & functional form
s5.blurb: Reading coefficients correctly: group gaps, interactions (DiD, different slopes, RDD), changing units, logs and standardized variables.
s5.metaphor: A dummy is a **light switch** (on = 1, off = 0). The reference group is **home base**: every dummy coefficient tells you how far that group sits from home base.

topics.title: Dummy variables and the reference group
topics.html:
With $J$ categories and an intercept, include $J-1$ dummies. The omitted one is the reference (benchmark) group, i.e. whoever has all the dummies $=0$.

$$\text{marks}=\beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{part\_time}+\beta_2\,\text{full\_time}+u$$
  • $\beta_0$ = mean for no job (the reference)
  • $\beta_1$ = part-time minus no-job; $\beta_2$ = full-time minus no-job
The dummy variable trap
All $J$ dummies + intercept: the dummies sum to 1 = the constant column, which is perfect multicollinearity. Fix it by dropping one category, or drop the intercept. Then each coefficient is that group's own mean (lecture: GE 102.29, GM 608.02, WH 42.89).

topics.title: Two dummies and their interaction
topics.html:
$Y=\beta_0+\beta_1D_1+\beta_2D_2+\beta_3(D_1D_2)+u$. The interaction is 1 only when both are 1. Plug in each case to get the four group means:

Try itThe 2×2 table of group means (KIELMC numbers)

$\beta_3$ is the extra effect when both switches are on: does the effect of $D_1$ depend on $D_2$?

topics.title: Difference-in-differences
topics.html:
$$\text{DiD}=(\bar Y_{T,after}-\bar Y_{C,after})-(\bar Y_{T,before}-\bar Y_{C,before})$$

Incinerator example: near-minus-far gap $=-18{,}824$ in 1978 and $-30{,}688$ in 1981, so DiD $=-30{,}688-(-18{,}824)=-11{,}864$. That is $\beta_3$ in reg rprice i.nearinc##i.y81.

Try itParallel trends picture (KIELMC, real means)
Identifying assumption
Parallel trends: without treatment, both groups would have changed by the same amount. The levels may differ (the first difference removes them).

topics.title: Dummy × continuous: different slopes
topics.html:
$$Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X+\beta_2D+\beta_3(XD)+u$$
GroupInterceptSlope
$D=0$$\beta_0$$\beta_1$
$D=1$$\beta_0+\beta_2$$\beta_1+\beta_3$

$\beta_2$ shifts the line; $\beta_3$ tilts it (the change in slope). Without $XD$, both groups are forced to share one slope.

Try itMove the dials

topics.title: Regression discontinuity (sharp RDD)
topics.html:
Treatment switches on at a cutoff of a running variable (age 21 for legal drinking). Center the running variable ($X_c=$ age − 21) and compare just below with just above:

$$Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X_c+\beta_2D+\beta_3(X_cD)+u$$

At $X_c=0$ the fitted values are $\beta_0$ and $\beta_0+\beta_2$, so $\beta_2$ is the jump at the cutoff ($\beta_3$ is the change in slope).

Try itMortality jumps at 21 (AEJfigs, real data)
Assumption
Without treatment, potential outcomes would change smoothly through the cutoff. Nothing else jumps at 21.

ChangeSlopese$t$, $p$, $R^2$
$Y^*=cY$$\times c$$\times c$unchanged

Wage example (bank Q19–20)
$\widehat{Wage}=-3.96+0.595\,Educ$ (hourly). Weekly wage $=40\times$ hourly, so the slope is $0.595\times40=23.8$. Education in decades: one more decade = 10 more years, so $0.595\times10=5.95$.
Exam trap
Ask "what does one new unit mean in old units?" A decade is 10 years, so multiply by 10. A month is 1/12 of a year, so divide.

topics.title: Logs and functional forms
topics.html:
FormModelRead $\beta_1$ as
Level–level$Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X$+1 unit $X$ → $\beta_1$ units $Y$
Log–level$\ln Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X$+1 unit $X$ → $\approx100\beta_1\%$ in $Y$ (exact: $100(e^{\beta_1}-1)\%$)
Level–log$Y=\beta_0+\beta_1\ln X$+1% $X$ → $\beta_1/100$ units $Y$
Log–log$\ln Y=\beta_0+\beta_1\ln X$+1% $X$ → $\beta_1\%$ $Y$ (elasticity)
Mnemonic
Log on $Y$ → think %. Log on $X$ → think "1%". Log–level: multiply by 100. Level–log: divide by 100. Log–log: read it as it is.
Try itInterpretation translator
Exam trap
$\ln(0)$ is undefined. Compare $R^2$ only between models with the same dependent variable (wage vs ln(wage) are different things to explain). Read the direction right: the right-hand variable changes and the left-hand one responds.

topics.title: Standardized coefficients
topics.html:
$$z_X=\frac{X-\bar X}{s_X}$$

If $Y$ and $X$ are standardized, a coefficient of 0.48 means +1 SD in $X$ → +0.48 SD in $Y$. That lets you compare regressors measured in different units (compare absolute values).

The intercept is ≈0 (all means are 0), and $R^2$, $t$ and $p$ are unchanged. It's only a rescaling, so it fixes no bias.

topics.html:
1. What's the dependent variable? Logged or not, standardized or not, units (ounces, \$/hour)?

  5. Translate into words with the right units and "holding other variables constant".

questions.q: Suppose $A$ is $2\times 3$ and $B$ is $3\times 2$. Which statement is correct?
